Topic 24 · Lab 2

One bad query, three symptoms

An online shop wants its top 100 customers by 2024 revenue, per tier and product category. The query joins four tables and it is slow. You will run it, read three symptoms in its Query Profile (no pruning, a heavy shuffle and skew), let the platform name them, fix the predicate alone to see why one change is not enough, then fix everything and prove it with an honest benchmark: same answer, a fraction of the time.

0Set up the environment5 min

What you are looking atA setup notebook creates the lab2402.shop schema with four tables of an online shop, 2023–2024: customers and products (5 M each at the default scale), orders (10 M) and order_items (about 55 M, with the order_date of its order). Three things are built in on purpose: every file of orders and order_items holds dates from both years, the dimensions are too big to broadcast, and 25% of the orders are guest checkouts, all under the placeholder customer customer_idx = 0, while 1% of the customers (the whales) place most of the rest.

MThe method, before you measure3 min

What you are looking atEvery step of this lab follows the same loop. The temptation is to jump straight to a fix (rewrite the join, add a hint, buy a bigger cluster) on a hunch. A wrong hunch costs days and can make things worse. So you look first, change one thing, and prove it.
1 · MeasureQuery Profile and system.query.history
→
2 · Name itFind the bottleneck (Performance Insights names it for you, where available)
→
3 · One fixOne change per round, or you will not know which one helped
→
4 · BenchmarkMedian of several runs, result cache off, cost and time
Two clocksThe Query Profile shows two durations. Wall-clock is what the user waited. Aggregated task time is the sum of the time of every task on every core: the work the platform did, and on serverless what you pay for. Task time is never below wall-clock. Much bigger means many cores worked at once. Close to it means the work went through a few tasks while the other cores waited: not always a problem, but it is exactly how skew looks.
No profile for cache hitsIf the result cache answers a query, no work happens and the Query Profile is not available. To measure, make every run really execute: a unique comment in the SQL text (what the benchmark helper does), or SET use_cached_result = false on a SQL warehouse. In system.query.history, from_result_cache = true gives a cache hit away. The disk cache is different: it keeps running and only changes the time, never what is pruned.
Before you tuneCheck what the platform already did for you: Photon (tasks time in Photon), AQE (the final plan) and, on managed tables, Predictive Optimization. Tune only the part they did not cover.

1Measure first: three symptoms8 min

What you are looking atRun the bad query once and read its Query Profile. You are looking for three things, and each one has its own view of the graph: the details panel for pruning, the Memory peak colouring for the shuffle, and the Rows colouring for the skew.
  1. Python
    %python
QUERY_A = """
-- A · the bad query, as someone wrote it: top 100 customers by 2024 revenue, per category
SELECT c.customer_id, c.tier, p.category,
       SUM(oi.quantity * p.list_price) AS revenue,
       COUNT(*)                        AS line_items
FROM lab2402.shop.orders o
JOIN lab2402.shop.order_items oi ON o.order_idx = oi.order_idx
JOIN lab2402.shop.products p     ON oi.product_idx = p.product_idx
JOIN lab2402.shop.customers c    ON o.customer_idx = c.customer_idx
WHERE date_format(o.order_date, 'yyyy-MM') BETWEEN '2024-01' AND '2024-12'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.tier, p.category
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 100
"""

display(spark.sql(QUERY_A))
    You should seeThe top 100 rows: revenue per customer, tier and category, highest first. The first rows belong to one "customer" of tier guest: the placeholder that holds every guest checkout.
  3. You should seeFiles pruned 0, although the query only wants one year out of two. The filter wraps order_date in a function, and the dates are mixed in every file anyway.
  4. You should seeThe darkest nodes are Shuffle nodes, and they lead the list with the most memory. The dimensions are too big to broadcast, so each of the three joins moves both sides across the network. Look at the Shuffle on oi.order_idx: all of order_items travels, both years, because the query filters orders and not order_items. Keep that in mind for block 4.
  5. You should seeThe darkest path is the order_items branch (about 55 M rows): that is the heavy shuffle again. The join with customers receives the 5 M orders of 2024 shuffled by customer_idx, and a quarter of them carry the same key, 0: they all land in one partition, so one task does the work of many. The Rows colouring shows how many rows go through each operator, not how they are split between tasks: block G shows the tool naming it.
    6. If something failsIf the Rows colouring does not make the hot path obvious, compare the two clocks in the details panel and the duration of the tasks of the stage: one task much longer than the median (5 times or more) is the skew.

GClick Optimize: two instructions from Genie Code4 min

What you are looking atYou have the symptoms. Now let the tool name them. Performance Insights (a preview) reads the profile for you and lists what it finds, and Optimize query hands the query, its profile and its insights to Genie Code, which answers with a recommendation in two instructions. You do not need to read every metric yourself: the tool reads them for you, you check its claim with a benchmark.
  1. Watch outPerformance Insights is a preview. If you do not see the light-bulb icon, a workspace admin enables it in Previews.
    You should seeDATA_SKEW on the Inner Join o.customer_idx = c.customer_idx: some tasks took much longer than the others. The recommendation lists the usual fixes: salting the hot key, a broadcast join for the smaller side, or pre-aggregating. The graph marks the operator with a red Recommendations tag. Symptom 3, named for you.
    2. Genie Code recommendationReplace date_format(order_date, 'yyyy-MM') BETWEEN … with a direct date range on order_date, then cluster the table on order_date to enable file pruning.
    4. Why two instructions?Instruction 1 removes the function, so the engine can use the per-file min/max. Instruction 2 reorders the data, so the files are organized by date. Without both, Files pruned stays at 0. Block 3 proves the first half: instruction 1 alone, and nothing is pruned.
    And the shuffle and the skew?Genie Code's two instructions are about reading. The insights named more: the data skew on the join with customers, with its usual fixes (salting, broadcast, or pre-aggregating). Block 4 applies the two instructions and goes after the shuffle and the skew.

2Benchmark A, honestly4 min

What you are looking atOne run proves nothing: on serverless, compute varies from run to run. An honest benchmark has four rules: bypass the result cache (a unique comment per run), discard a warm-up run, keep the median of several runs, and change one thing at a time. A is benchmarked now, on the layout it was written for.
  1. Python
    %python
benchmark("A", QUERY_A)
    You should seeFive timed runs and their median. The warm-up run is not printed in the median.
    2. Go and lookWant to see how the four rules turn into code? Open 2402-00 → 3 · Helpers used by the lab and read run_fresh() and benchmark(): about fifteen lines. run_fresh() writes the result to the noop sink: the whole query runs, but its rows are not brought to the notebook, so you time the engine and not the transfer of the result. The comment that run_fresh() appends, /* lab2402:A:run:… */, only changes the SQL text, so the result cache cannot match it.
    If something failsIf a run takes far longer than the others, that is exactly why we take the median. If all of them are slow because the workspace is busy, run the cell again later.

3Instruction 1 alone: fix the predicate5 min

What you are looking atOne change only: the filter on the raw order_date. The tables are still unordered. This is the "one change at a time" rule at work: you will see that this change, alone, is not enough.
  1. Python
    %python
QUERY_B = """
-- B · instruction 1: the filter on the raw column, nothing else changes
SELECT c.customer_id, c.tier, p.category,
       SUM(oi.quantity * p.list_price) AS revenue,
       COUNT(*)                        AS line_items
FROM lab2402.shop.orders o
JOIN lab2402.shop.order_items oi ON o.order_idx = oi.order_idx
JOIN lab2402.shop.products p     ON oi.product_idx = p.product_idx
JOIN lab2402.shop.customers c    ON o.customer_idx = c.customer_idx
WHERE o.order_date >= DATE'2024-01-01' AND o.order_date < DATE'2025-01-01'
GROUP BY c.customer_id, c.tier, p.category
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 100
"""

display(spark.sql(QUERY_B))
    You should seeFiles pruned is still 0. The engine can now use the min/max of every file, but every file spans both years, so no file can be skipped. That is the "why two instructions" of Genie Code, measured.
  2. Python
    %python
benchmark("B", QUERY_B)
    You should seeA median close to A's. One instruction alone does not change what is read, nor what travels.

4Everything right: layout, filter and aggregation8 min

What you are looking atQuery C asks exactly the same question as B and returns the same 100 rows. It keeps B's raw filter and changes three things, one for each symptom.
    4. In our run (<code>medium</code>)BC
    Files read / pruned96 / 073 / 41 (50% of the bytes pruned)
    Rows in the big shuffle (<code>oi.order_idx</code>)55 M: both years27.5 M: only 2024
    Join with <code>customers</code>5 M orders, 25% with the key <code>0</code>: one straggler task3.7 M rows already aggregated: no straggler
    Tasks total time34 s19 s
    Median of the benchmark10.0 s4.1 s
    Where the time goesMoving half the rows and removing the straggler task make most of the difference. Pruning files helps little in time here: reading was already cheap (Photon and the disk cache). Check each row of the table in the Query Profile of C.
  4. Python
    %python
for t in ["orders", "order_items"]:
    spark.sql(f"ALTER TABLE lab2402.shop.{t} SET TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.targetFileSize' = '{LAYOUT_FILE_SIZE}')")
    spark.sql(f"ALTER TABLE lab2402.shop.{t} CLUSTER BY (order_date)")
    spark.sql(f"OPTIMIZE lab2402.shop.{t} FULL")      # recluster the existing data, not only new files
    file_stats(t)
    You should seeBoth tables now report clustering ['order_date'] and many more, smaller files.
  5. Python
    %python
QUERY_C = """
-- C · everything right: raw filter on both tables, clustered layout,
--     and aggregate BEFORE the join with customers (the skewed one). Same answer as A.
WITH agg AS (
  SELECT o.customer_idx, p.category,
         SUM(oi.quantity * p.list_price) AS revenue,
         COUNT(*)                        AS line_items
  FROM lab2402.shop.orders o
  JOIN lab2402.shop.order_items oi ON o.order_idx = oi.order_idx
  JOIN lab2402.shop.products p     ON oi.product_idx = p.product_idx
  WHERE o.order_date  >= DATE'2024-01-01' AND o.order_date  < DATE'2025-01-01'
    AND oi.order_date >= DATE'2024-01-01' AND oi.order_date < DATE'2025-01-01'
  GROUP BY o.customer_idx, p.category
)
SELECT c.customer_id, c.tier, a.category, a.revenue, a.line_items
FROM agg a
JOIN lab2402.shop.customers c ON a.customer_idx = c.customer_idx
ORDER BY revenue DESC
LIMIT 100
"""

display(spark.sql(QUERY_C))
    You should seeThe same top 100 rows as A, guest first. In the profile, the three symptoms again: Files pruned 41 of 114 (half the bytes); the Shuffle on oi.order_idx moves 27.5 M rows instead of 55 M; and the join with customers now takes the 3.7 M rows already aggregated. The tasks total time drops from about 33 s to 19 s.
  6. Python
    %python
benchmark("C", QUERY_C)
    You should seeA median that is a fraction of A's: about 4 s against about 10 s in our run.
    7. One change at a time?B followed the rule and showed why one fix alone was not enough. C applies three fixes at once to reach the destination in one step. On your own queries, add them one by one and benchmark each: in this data, the layout alone prunes files but hardly moves the clock, while the filter on order_items and the early aggregation are what make it fast.

5The proof3 min

What you are looking atTwo questions, one cell: how much faster, and is it still the same answer? A rewrite that changes the result is not an optimization.
  1. Python
    %python
compare(QUERY_A, QUERY_C)
    You should seeA and B close to each other, C a fraction of A, and A and C return the same 100 rows: True.
    2. Keep going with Genie CodeThe Optimize query button in the Query Profile is only one door. The same assistant lives in notebooks and in the SQL editor, so you can use it well beyond reading profiles: ask it to rewrite a slow query, to explain a Query Profile you do not understand, or to suggest clustering keys for a table. Then do what this lab did: change one thing and prove it with an honest benchmark.
End of the labOne bad query, three symptoms, three fixes. No pruning came from the filter and the layout: the raw-column filter alone pruned nothing (B), it took the clustered layout too. The heavy shuffle came from tens of millions of order_items rows travelling to the joins: filtering order_items itself keeps them in the Scan. The skew came from one guest "customer" holding a quarter of the orders: aggregating before the join with customers leaves one row per customer and category, so the hot key no longer piles up in one task. Same answer, a fraction of the time, and every claim came with an honest benchmark.
